opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, and it gets at one of the central tensions in building these world models. The dynamics model is essentially trying to predict the next frame given some history of frames and actions, and the context window determines how much of that history it can actually condition on.

If you shorten the window, the most immediate effect is that the model has to lean much more heavily on the current frame, or the last couple of frames, to figure out what comes next. For a lot of local dynamics that's actually fine. If a character is jumping, you can infer a lot about where they're going from just the last few frames, because the motion is right there. So short-horizon physics and motion tend to hold up reasonably well.

Where you start to see problems is with anything that requires memory. If something goes off screen and then you turn back around, a model with a short context has no record of what was there, so it'll kind of hallucinate something plausible but not consistent. You lose object permanence, you lose consistency of the environment layout, and you can get this drifting effect where the world slowly morphs because nothing anchors it to what happened earlier.

There's also a subtler effect on how the model handles actions. Part of what lets the model learn a consistent effect for an action is seeing how that action played out over time. With less history, it can become harder to disambiguate things, like whether the camera moved or the object moved, so controllability can get a bit noisier.

On the flip side, a shorter context can sometimes make the model less prone to over-copying from the past. With very long contexts, models can get lazy and just reproduce earlier frames rather than really modeling the dynamics. So there's a trade-off: shorter windows force the model to actually reason about the transition, but at the cost of long-term coherence. In practice I think the interesting direction is finding ways to keep a compact memory, some kind of compressed representation of the past, so you get the consistency without paying for a huge raw frame history.

r001.rationale: The response says a shorter window means the model has less history to condition on and must rely more on the current or last few frames.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's actually something we thought about a lot with Genie. So the dynamics model takes in the history of frames, and the latent actions, and it has to predict what the next frame is going to look like. And the context window is really about how far back it can look.

If you shorten that context, I think the first thing you'd see is that the model would become much more reliant on the most recent frame or two, and it would lose a lot of its sense of memory. So things like an object that goes off screen and then comes back, or a character that moved behind something, the model just wouldn't have access to that information anymore. It would essentially have to hallucinate it, and you'd probably see more inconsistency over longer rollouts. Things would kind of drift.

The other side of it, though, is that with a very short context, the model is forced to lean more heavily on the latent action to explain what changed between frames, because it can't infer momentum or trajectory from a longer history. So in some ways you could imagine the latent actions becoming more informative, or at least the model attributing more of the change to them. But you'd pay for that in temporal coherence. In practice, the videos generated in Genie are fairly short anyway, so a lot of the dynamics are local, but I do think if you want to go to long-horizon generation, the length of that context, or finding some other way of keeping a persistent memory of the environment, is one of the key things you'd have to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says the context window determines how far back the model can look and that shortening it removes access to earlier frames.

astra-6.text: I’d expect it to rely more heavily on the most recent frames, because it no longer has access to that longer history. That might be fine if the recent frames contain enough information to predict what happens next. But if something important happened further back—say, an object moved out of view—it could have a harder time maintaining consistency. So shortening the window limits how far back the model can look; it doesn’t necessarily make it less dependent on the past frames it still sees.

r001.rationale: It says the shorter window means the model no longer has access to the longer history and limits how far back it can look.

sol-6.1.text: I’d expect it to rely less on distant past frames, simply because those frames are no longer available, and more heavily on the most recent observations. If that shorter window still contains enough information to infer things like velocity and direction, generation might work quite well. But if important information falls outside that window—say, an object was visible earlier and is now occluded—the model could lose track of it. So you might retain short-term plausibility while sacrificing some longer-term consistency.

r001.rationale: It says a shorter window leaves distant past frames unavailable, so the model relies less on them during generation.
